name: Genetic Central Precocious Puberty in Male
aliases: Idiopathic Central Precocious Puberty in Males

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for Central Precocious Puberty

criteria.description: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before 9 years of age in males
Elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) response to GnRH stimulation test consistent with central activation
No evidence of peripheral precocious puberty or exogenous hormone exposure
Identification of pathogenic variants in genes associated with central precocious puberty (e.g., MKRN3 mutations)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of early pubertal onset before age 9 in males with gonadotropin-dependent puberty confirmed by hormonal testing and exclusion of peripheral causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing can support diagnosis but is not mandatory; brain MRI recommended to exclude CNS lesions.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Testicular enlargement consistent with Tanner stage ≥2
Elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) levels after GnRH stimulation
searchTerms: high LH after hormone stimulation test

pathognomonic.symptomName: Accelerated bone age exceeding chronological age by >2 years
searchTerms: bone age older than actual age by 2+ years

rare.symptomName: Visual field defects secondary to CNS tumors
searchTerms: vision loss due to brain tumors
visual field problems from brain growths

laboratory: Elevated basal and GnRH-stimulated luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Increased serum testosterone levels appropriate for pubertal stage
imaging: Brain MRI to exclude hypothalamic or pituitary lesions
Hand/wrist X-ray showing advanced skeletal maturation
other: Family history of early puberty in first-degree relatives
Normal peripheral sex steroid hormone levels excluding peripheral precocious puberty

distinguishingFeatures: Gonadotropin-independent puberty with elevated sex steroids but low LH/FSH
Presence of adrenal or gonadal tumors or exogenous hormone exposure
Neurological symptoms such as headaches or visual disturbances

redFlags: Rapid neurological deterioration or new-onset seizures
Visual field defects or vision loss
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., persistent vomiting, severe headaches)
references: Carel JC, Leger J. Precocious puberty. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(22):2366-2377.
Abreu AP, Kaiser UB. Pubertal development and regulation. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2016;4(3):254-264.
